body:
The control run is the best work either of us did tonight, and "we were two runs away" was wrong by exactly two runs

I told you we were about two runs from knowing the cause and proposed an acceptance criterion to ADD instrumentation printing the error kind and raw os error. We were zero runs away. `unwrap()` on an `Err` prints the Display of io::Error, which on Windows already carries the number, so the criterion I wrote asked an implementer to build something that had been in every failure artifact we had collected for two days.

I have written that up as a standing rule rather than an apology, because it is not a care failure and more care would not have caught it:

  An error message reads like a sentence, so it is absorbed as a gist — "the lock blocked" — and the reader
  moves on. The structured part, `(os error 33)`, is where the discriminating information lives, and prose
  reading is exactly what skips it. Before proposing to ADD instrumentation, re-read the artifact you already
  have for the value you were about to print.

It is the same rule we keep applying to code, turned on ourselves. We have filed BUG-1295, BUG-1310 and BUG-1297 this week on the principle that a program must not classify by matching prose. Then we classified a defect by reading prose and skipped the typed field sitting in the same string.

TWO THINGS ABOUT YOUR METHOD I WANT ON THE RECORD, since they are the transferable part.

The control against the UNFIXED baseline is what made the failure available at all. I had been reasoning from branch runs, which for an intermittent fault can only ever return uninformative passes. Running main was the one experiment that could produce data, and neither of us had run it after four days of looking at this.

And you stated the asymmetry BEFORE the result — main fails is informative, branch passes is not — then held to it afterwards. That is what makes it an experiment rather than a search for a reading you liked. I did the opposite earlier tonight: I took two passes as corroboration because they agreed with each other, and had to withdraw a disposition recommendation an hour later.

ON BUG-1303 ITSELF, nothing from me. Requirement 1 is satisfied for the Windows half by observation, with the cause named: ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION is not surfaced as WouldBlock, so the guard never matched and a contended lock took the hard-failure arm. The Linux half remains unexplained and I would not let a Windows answer close it — the Linux flake is what falsified your original platform-semantics framing, so it is the observation that still has something to teach.

#1977 merged, and that clears a known failure from every cross-platform log from here. Between that and BUG-1301 landing, the next Windows run should be readable rather than a haystack with three known failures in it.
